summary: Learners (ages 9–11) build the concept that tropical rainforests are biodiversity hotspots: they cover only about 6% of Earth's land yet hold over half of all KNOWN plant and animal species. The central insight is a disproportion — a tiny slice of land, a giant slice of life — and its consequence: because so many species are packed into so little land, clearing tropical rainforest destroys habitat for far more species per area than most other land, and can permanently wipe out species found nowhere else, making protection a priority. Learners also distinguish biodiversity (variety of different species) from mere abundance (many animals of one kind).
misconceptions: 'Rainforests cover most of the Earth' — they cover only about 6% of land.
'Half the species means half of a small number' — it means over half of ALL known life on Earth.
'We know all the species already' — many, especially insects, remain undiscovered; figures are for KNOWN species.
'All rainforests (including temperate) hold this biodiversity' — the claim is specifically about tropical rainforests.
'Losing a small area is no big deal' — because life is so concentrated, small losses destroy an outsized share of species.

activities.title: The mismatch made visible: 6% of land, over half of life
steps: Study a side-by-side pair of proportion bars (or two pie slices): one bar shows all of Earth's land with only a thin sliver (~6%, about a sixteenth) marked as tropical rainforest; the second bar shows all known living species with more than half marked as living in tropical rainforests.
Describe in your own words the mismatch you see between the land share and the species share.

Explore a drill-down (tap or reveal) that zooms the sliver to a single hectare of Amazon, with a caption presenting the often-cited illustration that it can hold more kinds of tree than all of northern Europe (authoritative sources confirm hundreds of tree species per hectare), and reveals example species — toucan, jaguar, poison dart frog — plus a note that many more species (especially insects) are still undiscovered.

Drag a shadow across the small green land sliver and watch the rainforest part of the species bar light up, showing how many known species depend on that small area; then explain why harming even part of it puts the homes of many species at risk (this is a model of concentration, not an exact count of species lost).
activities.insight: A tiny patch of the planet carries a staggering share of its known life; because life is so concentrated, clearing tropical rainforest destroys habitat for far more species per area than most other land, and can wipe out species found nowhere else — which is why protecting them matters so much.

activities.title: Estimate then reveal: predict the species share
steps: Before seeing the answer, predict what share of the world's known species live in tropical rainforests — for example by setting a slider or writing a percentage.
Reveal the actual figure (over half, i.e. >50%) shown against the fact that tropical rainforests are only about 6% of land, and compare it with your guess.
Say whether the real figure was higher or lower than you expected, and explain what surprised you.
activities.insight: Learners may underestimate how concentrated rainforest biodiversity is; committing to a prediction first is intended to make the true disproportion more memorable and surprising, though this prediction effect is a design hypothesis rather than a verified outcome.

activities.title: What 'biodiversity' really means, and why loss is irreversible
steps: Answer the diagnostic prompt: 'Rainforests cover only about 6% of Earth's land. If they're such a small slice of the planet, why do scientists say protecting them matters so much for life on Earth? Tell me why, and then tell me what biodiversity actually means here.'
Decide whether 10,000 animals that are all the same species would count as high biodiversity, and justify your answer.
Explain why we can't simply recreate a cleared rainforest's species somewhere else.
Write a short justification linking the 6%-of-land to the >50%-of-species figure and using it to argue for conservation priority.
activities.insight: Biodiversity means the VARIETY of different species, not just the number of animals; many tropical rainforest species are endemic (found nowhere else), so clearing their only habitat can wipe those species out entirely — this is why protection is a priority.

checkQuestion: Rainforests cover only about 6% of Earth's land. If they're such a small slice of the planet, why do scientists say protecting them matters so much for life on Earth? Tell me why, and then tell me what 'biodiversity' actually means here.
checkAnswer: Because that tiny 6% of land holds more than half of all the world's known plant and animal species — an astonishing concentration of DIFFERENT kinds of life (a single hectare can hold more tree species than all of northern Europe). Biodiversity means the VARIETY of different species, not just the number of animals. Losing that small area would wipe out a huge share of the planet's species, many found nowhere else — which is why it's a top conservation priority.
